items.stem: A 20-year-old man comes to the emergency department 90 minutes after sudden onset of sharp right-sided pain and breathlessness. Both started while he was sitting at his desk at work. The pain is worse with deep breaths and has not eased with rest. He has no cough, fever, haemoptysis, leg swelling, recent travel or trauma. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and takes no medicines. He is 191 cm tall and weighs 68 kg. His temperature is 36.9 °C, pulse 104/min, respiratory rate 22/min, blood pressure 126/80 mm Hg and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He speaks in full sentences. The trachea is central and the jugular venous pressure is not raised. Over the right hemithorax, expansion is reduced, the percussion note is hyper-resonant and breath sounds are reduced. A 12-lead ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 104/min with no ST-segment or T-wave changes.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
items.explanation: This tall, thin young man who smokes has sudden one-sided pleuritic pain and breathlessness. He has reduced expansion, a hyper-resonant percussion note and reduced breath sounds on the right, so the most likely diagnosis is a primary spontaneous pneumothorax. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and needs decompression straight away, before any imaging. Here there are no features of tension: his blood pressure is normal, the trachea is central and the JVP is not raised. That means there is time to confirm the diagnosis. The first-line test is a standard erect posteroanterior chest radiograph taken in inspiration (BTS 2023, used in Australian EDs). It shows the visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it, lets you measure the size of the pneumothorax (2 cm or more at the hilum is large) and shows any mediastinal shift. Together with his symptoms, this guides the choice between observation, needle aspiration, an ambulatory device or a drain. CT is kept for unclear or complex cases.
why: An arterial blood gas does not confirm or size a pneumothorax, and with an oxygen saturation of 95% on room air it is not needed to assess his oxygenation.
CT pulmonary angiography involves radiation and contrast and looks for pulmonary embolism, which is unlikely here with no risk factors and clear one-sided signs of air in the pleural space.
Expiratory films are no longer recommended because they add little to detection over a standard inspiratory film and can make the size of the pneumothorax harder to judge.
A D-dimer is non-specific, does not confirm a pneumothorax, and should not come before imaging when the examination already points strongly to another diagnosis.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man sees his general practitioner because of 10 weeks of crampy right lower abdominal pain and four to six loose stools a day. Some stools are streaked by blood, and they wake him from sleep. He has lost 4 kg without trying and has had occasional night sweats. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and has taken ibuprofen most days for the pain. He has not travelled and has had no antibiotics in the past 3 months. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse 92/min and blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg. He is tender in the right iliac fossa, where there is vague fullness but no guarding. A soft perianal skin tag is present. Haemoglobin is 112 g/L (130–180), CRP 42 mg/L (<5) and albumin 31 g/L (35–50). Faecal calprotectin is 640 µg/g (<50). Stool bacterial and parasite PCR, culture and Clostridioides difficile toxin are negative.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanation: This young man most likely has ileocolonic Crohn's disease. The clues are a chronic history (over 6 weeks) of right iliac fossa pain, nocturnal diarrhoea with blood, weight loss, low-grade fever, a perianal skin tag, smoking, raised inflammatory markers, low albumin and a very high faecal calprotectin, with negative stool tests for infection. Under GESA and eTG guidance, diagnosis needs ileocolonoscopy, meaning colonoscopy that passes into the terminal ileum, with biopsies from the ileum and from each colonic segment, including normal-looking areas. This shows how far the disease extends and whether there are skip lesions or rectal sparing. Histology can show patchy transmural-type inflammation and non-caseating granulomas, and it can exclude intestinal tuberculosis, infection and malignancy. Small-bowel imaging is added after the diagnosis to stage the disease, not to make it. He should also stop ibuprofen and get urgent referral to gastroenterology.
why: Flexible sigmoidoscopy only reaches the distal colon, so it would miss ileocaecal disease, and the rectum and sigmoid are often spared in Crohn's disease.
MR enterography is useful for staging small-bowel extent, strictures and fistulae once the diagnosis is made, but it gives no tissue and cannot confirm the diagnosis.
Capsule endoscopy takes no biopsies and is not a first-line test, and an ileocaecal mass or stricture puts him at risk of the capsule getting stuck.
ASCA and ANCA serology has low sensitivity and specificity, so it cannot confirm or exclude Crohn's disease, and guidelines do not recommend it for diagnosis.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department with breathlessness and wheeze that began 6 hours ago, two days into a head cold. She has had asthma since childhood and uses only a salbutamol reliever. When she arrived 70 minutes ago, she could speak only in phrases and was using her accessory muscles. Since then she has had salbutamol 12 puffs and ipratropium 8 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes for three doses, prednisolone 50 mg orally, and oxygen by nasal prongs. She is alert but still speaks in phrases and uses her accessory muscles. Temperature is 37.4 °C, pulse 118/min, respirations 28/min, blood pressure 124/76 mm Hg and SpO2 94% on 2 L/min oxygen. There is widespread expiratory wheeze with equal air entry on both sides, and no rash or lip swelling. Venous blood gas: pH 7.44, pCO2 36 mmHg (reference 41–51), lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation, with no pneumothorax or consolidation. Salbutamol is being continued.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanation: This is severe acute asthma (she speaks only in phrases and uses her accessory muscles) that has not responded well to an hour of standard treatment. She has had repeated salbutamol and ipratropium by spacer, oral prednisolone within the first hour, and oxygen titrated to an SpO2 of 92–96%. The Australian Asthma Handbook and eTG advise adding IV magnesium sulfate (10 mmol over 20 minutes in adults) for severe or life-threatening asthma that responds poorly to the first bronchodilators. Salbutamol continues alongside it. She has no life-threatening features: she is alert, her SpO2 is 90% or above, her pCO2 is low rather than normal or rising, and her chest is not silent. So she does not yet need intubation, but she needs senior review and close monitoring. Aminophylline is not recommended in Australian guidelines because it adds little to standard treatment and causes arrhythmias, vomiting and seizures. IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or impending arrest, and she has no urticaria, angioedema or hypotension. IV hydrocortisone adds nothing when oral prednisolone has been given and can be swallowed. Antibiotics are not indicated, because the trigger is viral and there is no consolidation.
why: Aminophylline is not recommended in Australian guidelines: it gives little extra bronchodilation and has a narrow therapeutic index, with a risk of arrhythmias and seizures.
IM adrenaline is for anaphylaxis or near-arrest, and she has no urticaria, angioedema, stridor or hypotension.
She has already had oral prednisolone and can swallow; IV corticosteroid is no more effective and is only needed when oral intake is not possible.
A viral cold triggered this attack, and with no fever, purulent sputum or consolidation there is no indication for antibiotics.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 40 minutes after her horse fell on her during a trail ride, crushing the right side of her chest. She had right-sided pleuritic pain straight away and has become steadily more breathless during transport. She has no past medical history and takes only a combined oral contraceptive pill. On arrival she is agitated and can speak only in single words. Temperature is 36.4 °C, pulse 138/min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, and oxygen saturation 85% on 15 L/min via a non-rebreather mask. Her trachea is deviated to the left and her neck veins are distended. There is bruising and tenderness over the right lateral ribs. The right hemithorax is hyper-resonant to percussion, and breath sounds are absent on the right. Heart sounds are clearly audible. Two large-bore cannulae are in place and blood has been sent for group and hold. A mobile chest X-ray has been requested, and the radiographer will arrive in 10 minutes.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Portable chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis before any chest procedure
Subxiphoid pericardiocentesis guided by bedside ultrasound
Rapid sequence intubation followed by positive-pressure ventilation
Needle decompression at the fifth intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line
Intravenous bolus of 1 L warmed crystalloid over 15 minutes
items.explanation: This woman has a right tension pneumothorax after blunt chest trauma, with obstructive shock. She has hypoxia, tachycardia, hypotension, distended neck veins, tracheal deviation away from the injured side, and a hyper-resonant hemithorax with absent breath sounds. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. ATLS (11th edition) and eTG advise treating it as soon as it is recognised, without waiting for imaging. In adults, the preferred site for needle decompression is the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line, because the chest wall is thinner there and the catheter is more likely to reach the pleura than at the 2nd intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line. Finger thoracostomy at the same site is an acceptable alternative. After decompression, an intercostal catheter is placed in the safe triangle and connected to an underwater seal. A chest X-ray should be done only after that.
why: Wrong: tension pneumothorax is diagnosed clinically, and waiting 10 minutes for a film in a hypotensive, hypoxic patient risks cardiac arrest.

Wrong: tamponade is unlikely because her trachea is deviated, one side of her chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds, and her heart sounds are clear, so the chest needs decompressing rather than the pericardium.
Wrong: positive-pressure ventilation forces more air into the pleural space and can quickly worsen a tension pneumothorax and cause arrest if the chest has not been decompressed first.
Wrong: her shock is obstructive, not caused by blood loss, so fluid will not restore venous return while the tension pneumothorax is untreated, and giving it delays the treatment that saves her life.

items.stem: A 68-year-old woman is reviewed on the medical ward on day 3 of treatment for herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis, confirmed by CSF PCR. She has rheumatoid arthritis, and her weekly methotrexate has been withheld since admission. She weighs 70 kg and is receiving aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. She is still drowsy and has been drinking little. Her maintenance drip was taken down yesterday when the cannula tissued, and it was not restarted. Her urine output over the past 12 hours is 250 mL. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 98/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min and SpO2 97% on room air. Her mucous membranes are dry, and there is no new focal neurological deficit. Serum creatinine is 164 µmol/L (72 µmol/L on admission; reference 45–90), urea 11.8 mmol/L, sodium 140 mmol/L and potassium 4.6 mmol/L. Urine microscopy shows needle-shaped birefringent crystals.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Stop the antiviral and start oral valaciclovir 1 g three times daily
Stop the antiviral and start intravenous foscarnet
Continue the current regimen and add intravenous furosemide 40 mg
Arrange urgent haemodialysis through a temporary vascular catheter
Start isotonic crystalloid and reduce antiviral dosing to match renal function
items.explanation: This patient has acute kidney injury from aciclovir crystal nephropathy. Aciclovir is cleared by the kidneys and is poorly soluble in urine, so high-dose IV therapy in a dehydrated patient lets crystals form in the renal tubules. This is the main complication to prevent during treatment of HSV encephalitis, and it is why eTG advises keeping the patient well hydrated and monitoring renal function throughout. Her intake is poor, her drip has been stopped, she is oliguric with dry mucous membranes, her creatinine has more than doubled and her urine shows needle-shaped birefringent crystals. The right step is to restart isotonic IV fluids and adjust the aciclovir dose to her estimated creatinine clearance. Her Cockcroft-Gault clearance is about 30 mL/min, which calls for 10 mg/kg every 12 hours. IV therapy should continue for the full course, at least 14 to 21 days in an immunosuppressed patient, because stopping or under-treating HSV encephalitis carries high mortality and neurological morbidity. The injury usually reverses with hydration and dose adjustment. Methotrexate should stay withheld, because it is also cleared by the kidneys and would add toxicity.
why: Wrong: oral valaciclovir is not recommended for acute HSV encephalitis while the patient is drowsy and still in the IV phase, and it is converted to aciclovir, so it would not prevent crystal formation.
Wrong: foscarnet is reserved for aciclovir-resistant HSV and is more nephrotoxic, so it would make her kidney injury worse.
Wrong: furosemide would deepen her volume depletion and does nothing to clear crystals, and keeping full-dose aciclovir at this clearance would cause further accumulation and toxicity.
Wrong: she has no indication for urgent dialysis (no hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemic complications), and this injury usually reverses with hydration and dose adjustment.

items.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 11 pm by his mother with noisy breathing. He has had a runny nose and fever for 2 days, and this evening developed a barking cough and a hoarse cry. He is fully immunised and has no medical history. He weighs 12 kg. On arrival he was agitated, with stridor at rest, marked sternal and subcostal recession, and SpO2 91% in room air. He was given nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 (5 mL undiluted) and oral dexamethasone 7.2 mg (0.6 mg/kg), with oxygen held near his face. Sixty minutes later he is sitting on his mother's lap and playing. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 132/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and SpO2 97% in room air. He has an occasional barking cough, no stridor at rest and no chest wall recession. His mother would like to take him home now because his older sister is home alone with a neighbour.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Discharge home now with written advice on when to return
Obtain a lateral neck X-ray before deciding on discharge
Give a second nebulised adrenaline treatment before discharge
Observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline treatment
Arrange admission to intensive care for elective intubation
items.explanation: This child had severe croup: stridor at rest, a marked increase in work of breathing, agitation and hypoxaemia. Nebulised adrenaline works within minutes but wears off within about 2 hours. Dexamethasone takes several hours to reach full effect, so the obstruction can come back once the adrenaline wears off. The RCH Croup CPG says to observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose. Discharge is appropriate only if there is still no stridor at rest at that point, with clear safety-netting advice. The improvement at 60 minutes is likely the adrenaline effect and is not proof that the illness is settling. A mild tachycardia is expected after adrenaline. Discharging now risks the obstruction returning at home in the middle of the night. A lateral neck X-ray is not needed in typical croup, would not change management and could upset the child. Giving more adrenaline to a child with no stridor at rest has no benefit, and it would only restart the observation period. Intubation is for impending airway failure, such as exhaustion, ongoing hypoxaemia or repeated adrenaline needs, and this child has responded well.
why: Correct: the adrenaline effect lasts only about 2 hours, before the steroid has fully taken effect, so the RCH advises observing for at least 3 hours after the last dose and discharging only if there is still no stridor at rest.
Wrong: croup is a clinical diagnosis and this course is typical, so imaging would not change management and upsetting the child can worsen obstruction.
Wrong: adrenaline is given for severe obstruction such as stridor at rest with marked work of breathing, and has no preventive role in a child who has none.
Wrong: intubation is kept for a tiring child, ongoing hypoxaemia or repeated adrenaline needs, none of which this improving child has.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman comes back to her general practitioner 6 weeks after she was diagnosed with ulcerative colitis. Before the diagnosis she had 10 weeks of bloody, mucousy diarrhoea and left-sided abdominal cramps. Stool pathogen tests were negative. Ileocolonoscopy found continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to 30 cm and a normal proximal colon and terminal ileum. Biopsies showed crypt distortion with no granulomas and no dysplasia. She now takes oral mesalazine and mesalazine enemas. She has 1 to 2 formed stools a day with no blood. She has never smoked. Her mother was diagnosed with bowel cancer at age 62. No other relatives have had bowel cancer. Temperature is 36.7°C, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg and pulse 72/min. Her abdomen is soft and not tender. Haemoglobin is 129 g/L (115–165), CRP 3 mg/L (<5), ALP 74 U/L (30–110) and GGT 18 U/L (<40). She asks how her bowel cancer risk will be checked.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate surveillance plan for this patient?
options: Colonoscopy from 8 years after disease onset
Faecal immunochemical test every 2 years from age 45
CT colonography every 5 years starting now
items.explanation: Ulcerative colitis that reaches beyond the rectum raises the risk of colorectal cancer. Her colitis runs from the rectum to 30 cm, so it is left-sided (Montreal E2) and not proctitis alone. The risk depends on how long she has had colitis, how much colon is involved and how much inflammation there is. Cancer Council Australia and GESA recommend a first colonoscopy about 8 years after symptoms began. This colonoscopy restages the disease and uses chromoendoscopy or multiple biopsies to look for dysplasia. After that, the interval (1, 3 or 5 years) is set by risk factors such as ongoing inflammation, strictures, past dysplasia, PSC and family history. Her mother's cancer at 62 may shorten later intervals, but it does not change the start point. Population or family-history screening does not apply to her, because her colitis is the bigger risk and needs colonoscopy with targeted biopsies. Annual colonoscopy straight away is only for coexisting primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal ALP and GGT make this unlikely.
why: Colonoscopy every 5 years from 45 is family-history screening for a first-degree relative diagnosed under 55, which does not fit her history and starts too late for her colitis risk.
Two-yearly faecal immunochemical tests are average-risk population screening, and they cannot detect flat colitis-associated dysplasia or tell it apart from inflammatory bleeding.
Annual colonoscopy from diagnosis is for patients who also have primary sclerosing cholangitis, and her normal ALP and GGT make this unlikely.
CT colonography cannot take biopsies or show flat dysplasia, so it is not used for surveillance in inflammatory bowel disease.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 8 hours of constant, severe epigastric pain that radiates to her back, with repeated vomiting. The pain began 2 hours after a large evening meal. She drinks 2 standard drinks on weekends and does not smoke. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Her BMI is 34 kg/m2. Temperature is 37.6 °C, pulse 104/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min and SpO2 97% on room air. She has epigastric tenderness with voluntary guarding, no rigidity and no jaundice. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST changes. Results: lipase 2400 U/L (reference <60), white cell count 13.2 x10^9/L, CRP 40 mg/L, total bilirubin 22 µmol/L (<20), ALT 186 U/L (<35), ALP 140 U/L (30–110), corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L, triglycerides 1.8 mmol/L and creatinine 78 µmol/L. IV fluids and titrated opioid analgesia have been started.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the pancreas
items.explanation: She already meets 2 of the 3 criteria for acute pancreatitis: typical epigastric pain going through to the back, and a lipase more than 3 times the upper limit. The diagnosis is made, so the next step is to find the cause. Gallstones cause about half of all cases. An early ALT above about 150 U/L strongly suggests a biliary cause, and her obesity and diabetes add to the risk. Her calcium and triglycerides are normal and she drinks little alcohol. Australian guidance (eTG) and international guidance say every patient with acute pancreatitis should have a transabdominal ultrasound on admission to look for gallstones and a dilated bile duct. This is because a gallstone cause changes management: ERCP if there is cholangitis or a persisting duct stone, and cholecystectomy in the same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis. The test is quick, cheap, uses no radiation and can be done at the bedside. Early contrast CT does not help when the diagnosis is already clear. ERCP is for cholangitis or a proven obstruction that persists. MRCP and endoscopic ultrasound are second-line tests for when the ultrasound is unclear or no cause is found. Amylase adds nothing once the lipase is raised.
why: Contrast CT is for when the diagnosis is uncertain, or for looking for necrosis if she deteriorates after 72 hours; the diagnosis is already made, and CT in the first days underestimates necrosis and is poor at showing gallstones.
ERCP is invasive, carries a risk of making pancreatitis worse, and in the early phase is only for cholangitis or a proven persisting bile duct obstruction, neither of which has been shown here.
MRCP is a second-line test for suspected duct stones when the ultrasound is unclear or the liver tests stay abnormal; it should not come before the first-line ultrasound.
Amylase is less specific than lipase and clears sooner, so it adds nothing to a lipase already more than 30 times the upper limit and does not show the cause.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man who works as a mechanic sees his general practitioner because of tiredness for 4 months. He drinks about 4 L of water a day. He gets up three times a night to pass urine, even when he avoids drinks in the evening. He has gained 15 kg over 2 years and has not lost weight recently. He has hypertension treated with perindopril and takes no other medicines. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day. His father has type 2 diabetes. His temperature is 36.7 °C, pulse 82/min, blood pressure 138/86 mm Hg and respiratory rate 14/min. His BMI is 36 kg/m². He has velvety, darkened skin in both axillae and looks well hydrated. Urine dipstick shows glucose 3+, ketones negative, protein negative and specific gravity 1.025. A random fingerprick reading on the practice meter is 15.2 mmol/L.
items.ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
items.explanation: This man has the typical symptoms of hyperglycaemia: thirst, polyuria and nocturia that continues when he drinks less in the evening. He also has metabolic risk factors: obesity, acanthosis nigricans, hypertension, smoking and a family history of type 2 diabetes. His urine is concentrated and full of glucose, and he has no ketones, which points to type 2 diabetes. A fingerprick meter reading is not enough to diagnose diabetes, so the RACGP handbook and eTG require a laboratory test. HbA1c is the most appropriate test. A level of 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) or more diagnoses diabetes, he does not need to fast for it, and Medicare funds it for diagnosis. Because he has symptoms, one abnormal laboratory result is enough and no repeat test on another day is needed. A fasting or random venous plasma glucose would also be acceptable, but neither is among the options. An oral glucose tolerance test is kept for equivocal results or pregnancy. The water deprivation test, GAD antibodies and C-peptide do not confirm that he has diabetes.
why: An oral glucose tolerance test is kept for equivocal fasting (5.5 to 6.9 mmol/L) or random (5.5 to 11.0 mmol/L) glucose results or for pregnancy, and it is unnecessary and burdensome in a patient with symptoms and marked hyperglycaemia.

A water deprivation test looks for diabetes insipidus, but his urine is concentrated (specific gravity 1.025) and full of glucose, which shows an osmotic diuresis, and fluid restriction could make his dehydration worse.

GAD antibodies help classify suspected type 1 diabetes or latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (for example in a lean patient with weight loss or ketosis), but they do not confirm that diabetes is present.
C-peptide measures how much insulin the pancreas can still make and helps classify the type of diabetes, but it does not diagnose diabetes and can be misleadingly low during hyperglycaemia.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman comes to her general practitioner for her annual diabetes review. She has had type 2 diabetes for 14 years. Over the past 4 months, small print has become harder to read with her right eye, even with new reading glasses. She also has hypertension and dyslipidaemia. Her medicines are metformin 1 g twice daily, modified-release gliclazide 60 mg daily, perindopril 5 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. Her last eye examination was 2 years ago. A 59-year-old man sees his general practitioner with 4 months of tiredness and 3 kg of weight loss. Several times he has had a non-itchy rash on both shins that fades within a week. He has never had jaundice before and has never received blood products. He takes no regular medicines. Temperature is 36.8 °C, pulse 78/min and blood pressure 128/76 mmHg. His sclerae are icteric, there are spider naevi on his chest, the spleen tip is palpable, and there is palpable purpura on both lower legs. Investigations show:
Platelets 118 x10^9/L (150–400)
Bilirubin (total) 58 micromol/L (<20)
Albumin 30 g/L (35–50)
INR 1.4 (0.9–1.2)
HBsAg: not detected
Anti-HBs: 90 mIU/mL (protective ≥10)
Anti-HBc (total): not detected

HCV RNA: 2.1 x 10^6 IU/mL

In this man, HBsAg and total anti-HBc are not detected, and anti-HBs is 90 mIU/mL, above the protective level of 10 mIU/mL in the Australian Immunisation Handbook. The cause of his liver disease is chronic hepatitis C: a positive anti-HCV with detectable HCV RNA confirms current infection. His low albumin, raised INR, low platelets and splenomegaly suggest cirrhosis, and the palpable purpura suggests cryoglobulinaemic vasculitis (ASHM; GESA hepatitis C consensus statement).

Inactive chronic infection needs HBsAg to be present for more than 6 months, usually with anti-HBc and anti-HBe, and his HBsAg is not detected.
In the window period of acute infection, HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared, and anti-HBc IgM is positive; he has the opposite pattern, with anti-HBs present and no core antibody.
Occult infection means HBV DNA is detectable without HBsAg, and anti-HBc is usually present; his negative core antibody and protective surface antibody do not suggest it.
